The end of humans working in service industry? Theme park to open 'robot kingdom' where 200 androids make cocktails and food

Huis Ten Bosch is a curious but fun place I've often wanted to visit myself. An unusual kind of theme park that has intrigued me because it has had to reinvent itself repeatedly. It originated toward the end of the Japanese financial bubble as a simulation of a Dutch town appealing to the Japanese fascination with all things European. But what was unusual about it was that it was created as a live-in theme park. It featured an integral housing development where it sold and rented 'Dutch-style' houses along with a diverse shopping center. It was, after a fashion, akin to Walt Disney's original vision of Epcot (which stood for Experimental Prototype City Of Tomorrow) where the theme park would eventually be complemented by a planned community development. (which later turned into Celebration Florida) But when the Bubble burst, Huis Ten Bosch found itself in trouble and sought to adapt to survive with the development of attractions greatly diverging from its original Dutch village theme. It introduced haunted house attractions and puzzle/escape rooms. It developed a convention and meeting center. It adopted the One Piece anime as a theme and built its own version of the Thousand Sunny ship that sails around its bay. Recently, it added the Henn-Na Hotel or 'Strange Hotel' which attracted worldwide attention as the first hotel staffed by robots. Apparently that attention has convinced them to take the idea further and develop a theme park area based entirely on robots. It sounds like a lot of fun.

But Henn-Na was not so much about robots as a way to run a hotel as about robots as a novelty attraction for a hotel. I suspect this new theme park will be the same. It's not about automation doing anything practical, but about robots as an attraction. The real path of automation in accommodations is not robots greeting you at the check-in desk and carrying your luggage. It's about obsolescing that check-in desk altogether. It's about more subtle technology with far more disruptive impact. The real game-changer is the invention of the internet-enabled Smart Lock and its use with the concept of the Albergo Diffuso. That's Italian for 'dispersed hotel' and it originated with a plan to revitalize some dying medeival villages in Italy.

All across Europe--and particularly in Italy and Spain--there's been this problem of traditional towns dying as their farming and industry are obsolesced and younger populations move to the major cities. But these same towns are, actually, what tourists want to see and experience. Unable to win the interest of rich tourism developers, the government of one of these town hit upon a novel idea. Instead of trying to get someone to build a hotel for them, they would renovate the abandoned houses in the village and use them as rental suites, turning the whole village into a kind of hotel whose rooms were dispersed across the village. You would check-in/out at a central office and then go to your house or apartment. Most of the usual services of a hotel would still be available, but just dispersed, relying on the features of the town and things brought to the door.

With the advent of Airbnb this idea has, sort-of, gone global. But Airbnb is still missing a few key elements needed to make it truly convenient that are only now emerging. Even though it's 'online', it's still a very manual process--being designed around the idea of selling the spare room in people's homes. But what is coming is a new kind of Smart Lock technology that is integrated to the internet and mobile communications--allowing you to use your smartphone as a key. And so this means you can take any space anywhere in the world, put a Smart Lock on the door, and conduct that entire set of accommodations transactions--booking, payment, check-in/out, room services, housekeeping--entirely online or by smartphone. You can 'uberize' the whole thing.

So the way hotels are really going to be automated--quite soon--is not by replacing people with robots but rather by replacing keys with smartphones. The future hotel is a set of rooms with Smart Locks spread all over the world that you find, book, access, and pay for by smartphone and which have housekeeping and room service handled like Uber ride service. And this goes beyond just hotels. Whatever you can put a Smart Lock on, you can manage in a similar way; storage lockers, Automat-style cabinets for food, car rentals, subscription-access fitness centers and workshops, on and on.
Probably, but the quality of service will probably improve dramatically.
